Primary + Secondary: a dominant brand colour supported by secondary colours creates recognition with visual flexibility.
The 60 / 30 / 10 ratio is a starting point, and the balance can change according to the application.

rows.label: Icon & Logo
rows.text:
Upload your icon and logo in PNG or SVG formats, with a maximum file size of 50 KB each.
SVG: a vector file: stays sharp at any size and is tiny, so it is the best format for a logo or icon on screen and on the web.
PNG: a pixel image with a transparent background: use it when you only have the logo or icon as an image, at a large enough size to stay sharp.
PDF: a vector file for print: the format printers and sign makers usually ask for, so keep one for business cards, signage and merchandise (upload the SVG or PNG here).
Choose an icon and logo that represent your organisation clearly and consistently.
Circle: unity, community, harmony and continuity.
Square: stability, structure, reliability and balance.
Rectangle: order, practicality, structure and professionalism.
Triangle: direction, progress, strength and movement.
Hexagon: balance, connection, efficiency and structure.
Organic shapes: natural, friendly, creative and approachable.
Abstract shapes: distinctive, conceptual and open to interpretation.
These are common visual associations, and context shapes what each one means.
Icon vs Logo: the icon should remain recognisable at small sizes, while the logo can combine the icon with the organisation name.

rows.label: Typography
rows.text:
Choose typefaces that support your brand's character while remaining appropriate for their intended use.
Serif: letters with finishing strokes, often giving a traditional, editorial or refined feel. E.g. Georgia, Garamond, Times New Roman.
Sans-serif: letters without finishing strokes, often giving a modern, clear and straightforward feel. E.g. Inter, Helvetica, Arial.
Slab serif: serif typefaces with thick, block-like finishing strokes, often giving a strong, solid and distinctive feel. E.g. Rockwell, Roboto Slab.
Script: typefaces inspired by handwriting or calligraphy, often giving a personal, elegant or expressive feel. E.g. Pacifico, Dancing Script.
Display: typefaces designed for visual impact at larger sizes, often used for headlines, titles and short statements. E.g. Bebas Neue, Abril Fatface.
These categories describe common visual characteristics and associations, and context shapes what each one means.
Use complementary typefaces and prioritise readability over personality.
Serif + Sans-serif: Georgia + Inter creates classic headings with clean, modern body text.
Display + Sans-serif: Abril Fatface + Inter creates expressive headings with clear supporting text.
Sans-serif + Sans-serif: Montserrat + Open Sans creates a clean, contemporary system with subtle contrast.
Serif + Serif: Garamond + Georgia can create an editorial feel when each has a distinct role.
Single typeface family: Inter Regular + Inter Bold creates a simple, consistent system from one typeface, with weight giving the contrast.
Readability: use highly expressive typefaces selectively and prioritise clear, comfortable reading for body text and interface content.
Recommended: use 1–2 typefaces for most brands; use 3 only when each has a clearly defined purpose.

rows.label: Text Hierarchy
rows.text:
Use larger sizes for more important headings, and smaller sizes for longer text to keep it comfortable to read.
H1 (Title), 36–48 px: the title of a page or document.
H2 (Section), 28–36 px: the headings of its sections.
H3 (Subsection), 22–28 px: the headings within a section.
Body Text, 16–18 px: paragraphs and anything read at length.
Captions & Metadata / Interface, 12–14 px: captions, dates and labels, and the text of an interface.
Maintain a clear and consistent relationship between text levels.
Use size and weight to distinguish levels, keep similar content at the same level, and avoid creating unnecessary text levels.

rows.label: How will you stand apart?
rows.text:
What the offering does differently from the competitors: where it hits exactly the blind spot they leave.
Started from the openings you ticked on your Competitors (What could you do differently?); change it freely.
It is about the offering; the result the buyer gets from it is asked on each Offering.
Cost-driven (saving resources): targets the blind spot of expensive competitors with a budget-friendly alternative.
Convenience-driven (speed and ease): targets the blind spot of complex or slow solutions.
Compliance, Risk & Security: targets the blind spot of uncertified or questionable alternatives.
Status & Premium (exclusivity): targets the blind spot of mass-market or cheap products with top quality and custom service.
Performance & Innovation (product superiority): targets the blind spot of dated or underpowered alternatives with better results and newer methods.
Ecosystem & Integration (fits what they already use): targets the blind spot of standalone tools cut off from the buyer's other systems and workflows.
Personal Service & Relationship (customer intimacy): targets the blind spot of impersonal providers with a service shaped around each customer.
At this stage (Planning): choose one. When the stage changes (the Opening Date), an answer over the limit goes back to empty.
Based on: Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness (n.d.) Strategic Positioning. Boston, MA: Harvard Business School. Available at: https://www.isc.hbs.edu/strategy/business-strategy/Pages/strategic-positioning.aspx (Accessed: 25 October 2026).
Also: Loy, T. (2007) E145 Technology Entrepreneurship, Session 6: Entrepreneurial Marketing. Stanford, CA: Stanford University. Available at: https://web.stanford.edu/class/e145/2007_fall/startup_mktg_details.shtml (Accessed: 25 October 2026).

rows.label: What does this person want to achieve?
rows.text:
1 = Minor, 5 = Main.

Accessibility: getting something hard to reach. Development: learning something new. Expression: showing who they are. Revenue: winning customers or income.

Resolution: getting a specific problem fixed. Enjoyment: having fun or a good time.

Cost: too costly, or unclear prices. Delays: it takes too long. Inconsistency: results vary. Trust: hard to find someone reliable.

rows.label: Relationship Type
rows.text:
Self-Service: The customer can find information, make decisions and use the offering independently, with little direct assistance.
Personal Assistance: A person communicates directly with the customer and provides guidance or help when needed.
Dedicated Support: The customer receives structured, ongoing support from a designated person or team.
Community: The relationship is supported through interaction with a community of customers or users.
Automated Service: Technology provides information, guidance or assistance without direct involvement from a person.

rows.label: Customer Source
rows.text:
Referrals: Customers introduced by clients, partners or a network.
Sales funnel: Customers found through outreach: prospects, some of them qualified, some of those buying.
Repeat customers: Customers already won who buy again. Count the repeat purchases only, never the customers a second time. An established business can enter its repeat sales a month directly.
Contracts or tenders: Work won by bidding or proposing: tenders, pitches, framework contracts.
Marketplace or walk-in: Customers who find you: a shop, a stall, a marketplace listing, a website.
Other: Any other source, such as customers moving on from another Offering: enter the figure and say what it rests on.

rows.label: Active clients
rows.text:
Formula: Active clients = New clients a month ÷ Cancel%
At the steady level, clients joining each month equal clients leaving. Average client lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ Cancel%.
Based on: Gupta, S. et al. (2006) ‘Modeling Customer Lifetime Value’, Journal of Service Research, 9(2), pp. 139–155. Available at: https://www.anderson.ucla.edu/sites/default/files/documents/areas/fac/marketing/JSR2006(0).pdf (Accessed: 29 September 2026).

rows.label: Community
rows.text:
Community: Spaces where people gather to discuss, participate, share knowledge and interact with your organisation or community.
Social Media: Social platforms where people can discover your organisation, engage with your content and stay connected.
Website: Your organisation's own website and pages, used to present information, offerings, transactions, delivery or support.
Marketplace: Third-party platforms where customers can discover, evaluate, purchase or receive your offerings.
In Person: Physical locations, meetings, events or activities where you interact directly with customers.
Email: Communication with customers through email, including direct messages, newsletters and follow-ups.
Online / Live: Live digital interactions or experiences delivered through online meeting, streaming or communication platforms.
Direct Payment: Methods customers use to pay your organisation directly, such as cash, card or bank transfer.
File Delivery: Services or methods used to deliver digital files or downloadable products to customers.
Physical Delivery: Methods used to physically deliver products to customers, such as courier, postal service or local delivery.
Retail & Wholesale: Shops, stockists and trade buyers who sell your offerings to their own customers, or buy them in bulk to resell.
Referral & Affiliates: People and partners who send customers to you and are rewarded for the sales or leads they bring.
Other: A channel that does not fit any of the categories above.

rows.label: Costs
rows.text:
Cost: Money the organisation needs to spend.
Cost Group says what a cost supports; Behaviour says how it changes with activity; Frequency says when it is paid. They are three different things.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Launch budget
rows.text:
What is spent before the opening: capital expenditure (assets) + startup expenses + pre-operating expenses. Opening stock is apart.
Capital expenditure is an asset, depreciated; startup and pre-operating expenses are expensed.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Running costs a month
rows.text: The fixed costs of a month of operation, from the opening (OpEx). They set the cash buffer: the launch budget plus months of running costs.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Cost of each sale
rows.text: The variable costs that move with sales (COGS): prices per unit, and costs that are a percent of revenue. They decide the break-even.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Group
rows.text:
Establishment: Costs required to establish or launch the organisation.
Operating: Ongoing costs that keep the organisation functioning, independently of any one Offering.
Offering: Costs of creating, delivering or supporting a particular Offering.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page
Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Launch: before the opening
rows.text: Costs dated before the Opening Date: capital expenditure (assets), startup expenses and pre-operating expenses. They make the Total Pre-operational Budget.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Running costs: every month
rows.text: Fixed costs that recur after the opening, as a monthly equivalent. They set the cash buffer: one-time costs plus months of running costs.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Cost of each sale
rows.text: Variable costs that move with sales (cost of goods sold): a price per unit or a percent of revenue. They decide the break-even.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: One-time costs after the opening
rows.text: One-time costs paid from the opening on. They are in the Funding Need of their group.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Funding Need
rows.text:
Funding Need: Money the organisation needs to obtain to support its financial requirements.
A need can be one amount by one date, or several amounts over time.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page
Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Establishment
rows.text: Money required to establish and launch the organisation.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Operating
rows.text:
Money required to support operations before revenue becomes sufficient: the running costs, only until revenue covers them.
Lenders also call this working capital.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Loan Repayments
rows.text:
SBA Microloan (Requested / Applied): its $470 monthly repayments are not counted until it is approved.
Only loans that are Approved / Agreed, Received / Available or Completed / Closed are repaid in this table. A pending loan's repayments are counted only with the funding being sought: in Financial Position below, and in the Stress Test on Sustainability.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Offering
rows.text: Money required to develop, prepare or launch an Offering before it can generate sufficient revenue.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Cash to raise before the opening
rows.text: The Total Pre-operational Budget (CapEx, Startup Expenses and Pre-Operating Expenses dated before the Opening Date) plus the Startup Contingency Fund, plus the cash for opening inventory, which is added after the contingency and is not part of its base.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Operational Contingency Fund
rows.text: After the launch, each month a share of OpEx is set aside on top of the startup fund, until the fund equals the target reserve months of OpEx. The contribution is a cash set-aside, held as savings. The rates and the target are in the Global Settings.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Capital & Funding
rows.text:
Capital: Money contributed to the organisation, particularly by founders or investors.
Funding: Financial resources provided by another source to support the organisation.
Loan: Borrowed money that creates a repayment obligation.
Revenue: Money generated through the organisation's Offerings. Capital and funding are not revenue.
Expected, confirmed and available money are different: only money that has arrived counts as money the organisation has.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Internal
rows.text: Money from inside your organisation: its founders' capital, reinvested revenue or funds it already holds.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Status
rows.text:
Planned: Identified, waiting to be pursued.
Preparing: An application or proposal is being prepared.
Requested / Applied: Asked for; no answer yet.
Approved / Agreed: Confirmed, but not all of it has arrived.
Received / Available: The money has arrived and can be used.
Completed / Closed: Fully received; nothing more to come.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page
Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Received So Far
rows.text: How much has actually arrived. The rest counts as confirmed future money.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Funding Schedule
rows.text:
One-time: A single payment.
Periodic: A repeated amount at a set frequency.
Milestone-based: Released as defined milestones or conditions are reached.
Other: An arrangement that fits none of the above.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: External
rows.text:
Non-repayable: Grants, subsidies and awards: nothing to repay, though often with conditions.
Equity: Investment in exchange for a share of ownership.
Debt: Loans and credit that must be repaid, with interest.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Loan Start
rows.text: When the loan is paid out.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Repayment Method
rows.text:
Equal payments: The same payment every time; the interest part shrinks as the loan is repaid.
Equal principal: The same amount of principal every time, plus that period's interest, so payments fall over time.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Loan repayment
rows.text:
Formula: Payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n) (annuity); equal-principal: P ÷ n plus interest
A fixed payment that covers interest and repays the loan over n periods; r is the interest rate for one period (for monthly payments, the monthly rate).
Source: Gutierrez, P.H. and Dalsted, N.L. (2012) Long Term Loan Repayment Methods. Fort Collins, CO: Colorado State University Extension. Available at: https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/long-term-loan-repayment-methods/ (Accessed: 29 September 2026).
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Other
rows.text: Reward crowdfunding, friends & family, in-kind contributions and other arrangements.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Financial Position
rows.text:
Funding Gap: The amount of identified financial requirement not covered by available or confirmed financing.
Financial Runway: The estimated period for which available financial resources can support the organisation under current assumptions.
Every figure here is an estimate based on the information entered, not financial advice.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Available Now
rows.text: Financial resources that have arrived and can be used.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Confirmed Future
rows.text: Confirmed, but not yet available.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Pending
rows.text: Expected and awaiting confirmation; the gap and the runway count it once it is confirmed.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Funding Gap
rows.text:
Funding Gap: The amount of identified financial requirement not covered by available or confirmed financing.
Formula: Funding gap = Funding needed − Funding available and confirmed
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Financial Runway
rows.text:
Financial Runway: The estimated period for which available financial resources can support the organisation under current assumptions.
Counts money available now and confirmed money as it is scheduled to arrive, against every scheduled cost and loan repayment, with the revenue expected on Sustainability as it is received.
Formula: Runway = Cash ÷ Monthly net burn (here: the first month the projected balance goes below zero)
Based on: Damodaran, A. (2016) The Bonfire of VC: Cash Burn, the Good, the Bad & the Ugly. New York: NYU Stern School of Business. Available at: https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/pdfiles/blog/CashBurn.pdf (Accessed: 29 September 2026).
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Funding Need Coverage
rows.text: Confirmed and available funding linked to each need under Capital & Funding.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Funding Mix
rows.text: Where the financial resources originate, confirmed and pending.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Funding Timeline
rows.text: Money in and out of your organisation month by month, and the balance it leaves. A dip below zero is a cash-pressure period, even when the totals are sufficient.
scenes: Business System / Financial Foundation / page

rows.label: Upcoming Obligations
rows.text: Significant money in or out over the next six months.

rows.label: Frequency
rows.text: The period of the salary and of both hours: a week, a month or a year, whichever you know. Every calculation turns them into a month: a week's at 52 ÷ 12 ≈ 4.33 weeks a month (40 h a week is about 173 h a month), a year's divided by 12.

rows.text:
Revenue Partners: Parties who sell for you or send customers, and take a cut of each sale, e.g. Boutique stockist, Distributor, Referral partner, Affiliate blogger, Co-teacher.

rows.label: Suppliers
rows.text:
Goods & Equipment: Sellers of furniture, devices and consumables for the company, e.g. Furniture dealer, Stationery merchant, Computer reseller, Water-cooler rental.
Business Services: Firms that run the administrative side, e.g. Accountant, Lawyer, Insurance broker, Payroll bureau, Business bank, Web host.
Creative & IT Services: Freelancers and small agencies for design, branding, content or technology work, e.g. Web builder, Brand identity house, Photographer, IT support, Copywriter.
Property, Vehicles & Facilities: Owners and caretakers of the premises, and lessors of vehicles, e.g. Landlord, Coworking operator, Cleaner, Car lessor.
Technical Support: Outsourced technicians who maintain, repair and install the company's assets, e.g. Electrical engineer, Plumber, Boiler fitter, Network cabling. An installation is linked to the asset it installs.

rows.label: Suppliers
rows.text:
Producers & Wholesalers: Producers and wholesalers that sell the materials and parts in the product, e.g. Wool mill, Box maker, Fabric importer, Flour miller.
Contractors & Advisers: Outsourced specialists who do part of an offering's job or guide it, e.g. Dye works, Freelance developer, Product-safety adviser, Electrician.
Agencies & Influencers: Firms and creators paid to spread the word, e.g. Marketing agency, Instagram creator, Poster press, Podcast sponsor.
Venues & Organisers: Hosts of the places and events where you sell, e.g. Fair organiser, Exhibition hall, Show promoter.
Landlords, Leasing & Warehouses: Owners of premises used for making or storing stock, and lessors of vehicles, e.g. Estate owner, Depot firm, Chilled-storage outfit, Van leasing specialist.
Platforms & Payments: Intermediaries between you and the customer who charge a fee, e.g. Online marketplace, Payment processor, App store, Reservation portal.

rows.label: Begins and Payment
rows.text:
Revenue begins after the sales cycle, the time from first contact to a signed sale: for services to businesses it is often 4 to 12 weeks.
One sale often leads to another, such as a build after an audit: start the later stream when the first ones finish.
Money arrives when the customer pays, which can be well after the sale: invoices are often paid 30 days after they are sent, and some later.

rows.text: From this Offering's Demand & Conversion on Customer Engagement: Other: estimated at 0.3 new a month. Referrals: 0.5 referrals a month, 40% buy: about 0.2 new a month. Together about 0.5 new a month. With 10% cancelling a month, they level off at about 5 active clients, reached in about 22 months.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: First Month
rows.text: How many clients in the month revenue begins.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Revenue Summary
rows.text: Expected revenue at the normal operating level, a month.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Can the Expected Sales Be Delivered?
rows.text:
Capacity is the founders' delivery hours a month: the time the organisation controls.
Needed: each month's expected sales times each founder's Working Hours per Unit (4. Delivery, on Infrastructure & Capability).
Recurring work (subscriptions, retainers) is served first; what remains is flexible capacity for the other Offerings.
External professionals' hours are delivered outside this capacity; their cost is part of the Offering's costs.
A shortfall does not change the sales forecast: it says more capacity may be needed.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Capacity used
rows.text:
Formula: Utilisation = Demand hours ÷ Available hours
How much of the available time the planned work needs. Above 100% means more work than capacity.
Based on: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (2026) Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization (G.17): About. Available at: https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g17/About.htm (Accessed: 29 September 2026).
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Break Even
rows.text:
Break-Even Point: The level of revenue or activity at which revenue covers costs.
Break-Even Time: When the organisation is expected to reach that level.
Financial Exhaustion: When available resources are expected to run out, with expected revenue included.
All results are estimates based on the assumptions entered, not guarantees.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Expected Monthly Revenue
rows.text:
Formula: Σ price × expected sales per month, for each Offering
The revenue the expected sales bring in a normal month.
Calculated from your Offerings' prices and expected sales.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Break-Even Revenue
rows.text:
Fixed costs divided by the contribution margin of the expected revenue mix.
Formula: Break-even revenue = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution margin ratio
Source: U.S. Small Business Administration (n.d.) Calculate your startup costs: break-even point. Available at: https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/plan-your-business/calculate-your-startup-costs/break-even-point (Accessed: 29 September 2026).
Also: Franklin, M., Graybeal, P. and Cooper, D. (2019) ‘3.2 Calculate a Break-Even Point in Units and Dollars’, in Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting. Houston, TX: OpenStax, Rice University. Available at: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/3-2-calculate-a-break-even-point-in-units-and-dollars (Accessed: 29 September 2026).
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Expected Break Even
rows.text: The first month revenue covers costs, based on the build-up of sales you entered.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Financial Exhaustion
rows.text:
When available cash is expected to run out: funding received or confirmed on Financial Foundation, plus expected revenue as it is received.
Funding still expected or applied for is not counted until it is confirmed.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Sustainability Buffer
rows.text: Financial Exhaustion minus Break-Even Time: how much time exists between becoming sustainable and running out of resources.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Costs Used
rows.text:
Read from Financial Foundation, by behaviour.
Fixed: the monthly equivalent of every recurring cost, plus loan interest. Loan principal is repayment of borrowed money, kept outside the costs; one-time costs are what the funding is for.
Variable: per-unit and per-project costs linked to each Offering.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Break-Even Point
rows.text:
Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit.
Offering break even: the units this Offering alone would need to sell to cover all fixed costs.
Organisation break even: the expected revenue mix, scaled as a whole until its contribution covers the fixed costs.
Formula: Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ (Price − Variable cost per unit)
Source: U.S. Small Business Administration (n.d.) Calculate your startup costs: break-even point. Available at: https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/plan-your-business/calculate-your-startup-costs/break-even-point (Accessed: 29 September 2026).
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Each Offering's Costs
rows.text:
An Offering's costs are those recorded for it on 3. Infrastructure & Capability → Offering's Capability.
Per sale: paid for every unit or project sold. Contribution is what is left of the price after them.
Whatever is sold: paid monthly or once, however much is sold. After them, what the Offering adds towards the organisation's shared costs.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Contribution
rows.text:
Formula: Contribution = Price − Variable costs; ratio = Contribution ÷ Price
What each sale leaves to pay fixed costs and profit.
Source: Franklin, M., Graybeal, P. and Cooper, D. (2019) ‘3.1 Explain Contribution Margin and Calculate Contribution Margin per Unit, Contribution Margin Ratio, and Total Contribution Margin’, in Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting. Houston, TX: OpenStax, Rice University. Available at: https://openstax.org/books/principles-managerial-accounting/pages/3-1-explain-contribution-margin-and-calculate-contribution-margin-per-unit-contribution-margin-ratio-and-total-contribution-margin (Accessed: 29 September 2026).
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page
Business System / Sustainability / page
Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Break-Even Time
rows.text: The first month in which expected revenue covers that month's costs: the fixed costs, and the variable costs of that month's volume.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Revenue-Adjusted Financial Position
rows.text:
The Financial Foundation timeline with expected revenue received and variable costs paid as they are expected.
Funding runway (Financial Foundation, without revenue): 1 month.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Stress Test
rows.text:
The plan as it stands, and the same plan when things go worse than hoped: sales 20% lower, revenue 3 months later, costs 10% higher (founders' pay aside), customers paying a month later than planned, and all four together.
The funding being sought is counted as if it arrives as planned, its repayments included: the question a lender asks is whether the plan holds with the money requested.
Holds: cash stays at zero or above throughout the plan. Short: how much more money would keep it there.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: What It Would Take
rows.text:
Worked out from the plan: the smallest single change that keeps the cash at zero or above in every month of the plan, each tried on its own with everything else as planned.
The funding being sought is counted as if it arrives as planned, its repayments included, as in the Stress Test.
Where the plan already holds, it says how far sales, the start of revenue or costs could go against it instead.
scenes: Business System / Sustainability / page

rows.label: Global Settings
rows.text: The rates and limits the calculated lines use. Change one here and every line that uses it follows.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Plan Start
rows.text:
Month 1 of the financial plan. Every timeline on the Financial Foundation and on Sustainability runs from it.
Worked out: the earlier of the Opening Date's month (set on the Organisation tile) and the month of your earliest cost, a costed card or a legal expense, whichever was recorded first.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Plan Length
rows.text: How far ahead the plan looks. Lenders usually ask for the first year month by month and a profit and loss forecast for three years.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Amounts
rows.text:
Excluding Sales Tax: Registered to collect Sales Tax: amounts exclude it. The tax collected is paid to the state and is not revenue.
Including Sales Tax: Amounts are gross, as paid and charged.
Not registered for Sales Tax: No Sales Tax is charged; Sales Tax paid on purchases is part of their cost.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Income Tax
rows.text: Income tax on profit. Pass-through businesses (e.g. most sole traders and single-member LLCs) pay it personally, on the owner's own tax return. For a company, enter the corporate rate; ask your accountant.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Business stages
rows.text:
Today: Planning. Planning: 2 months to the Opening Date (1 Feb 2027). Planning is meant to take 3 months.
Set by the Opening Date and the durations below: planning before the opening, then launching, managing and growing, each for the time set here. Change the Opening Date, or a duration, to change the stage.
The four stages are those of the US Small Business Administration's business guide.
Planning: How long the planning is meant to take, counted back from the Opening Date (the Review says when it has run longer). A business with no Opening Date yet is planning.
Launching: From the Opening Date: the first customers, the MVP, the proof that the market accepts it. The Early Positioning Statement is proved or changed within it.
Managing: After Launching: stabilising, keeping customers, product-market fit. The Core Market Positioning stands for it.
Growing: After Managing: scaling and expanding into new markets. The Corporate & Portfolio Positioning looks as far ahead.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Opening Date
rows.text:
The day the business opens and issues its first receipt. It sets the stage: planning before it, launching from it.
The stage also sets Positioning's name and how many choices its questions allow; a change of stage empties an answer over the new limit.
Costs dated before it make the pre-operational budget, on the Financial Foundation.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Planning duration
rows.text: How long the planning is meant to take, counted back from the Opening Date (the Review says when it has run longer). A business with no Opening Date yet is planning.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Launching duration
rows.text: From the Opening Date: the first customers, the MVP, the proof that the market accepts it. The Early Positioning Statement is proved or changed within it.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Managing duration
rows.text: After Launching: stabilising, keeping customers, product-market fit. The Core Market Positioning stands for it.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Growing duration
rows.text: After Managing: scaling and expanding into new markets. The Corporate & Portfolio Positioning looks as far ahead.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Employer on-cost coefficient
rows.text: Added to the gross salaries, for the country. It differs by country.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Insurance per employee
rows.text: An amount a month, for key-person and health cover.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Corporate income tax rate
rows.text: A rate on net profit.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Capitalisation limit
rows.text: A purchase of one unit at or above it is CapEx; below it, OpEx.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Useful Life
rows.text:
What it is: The years an asset serves the business before it is worn out, outdated or replaced.
What it does: The cost (CapEx) is spread over those years, a share in each year of use.
A group has one useful life in years; an asset of the group can have its own under it, and an empty one takes the group's.
Source: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services (2011) ‘Appendix B: State Property Class Codes’, in Asset Management Handbook. Austin, TX: Texas DFPS. Available at: https://dfps.texas.gov/handbooks/Asset_Management/Files/ASM_px_2.asp (Accessed: 10 October 2026).
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Royalty on sales
rows.text: The default rate; a card may set its own for its contract.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Affiliate network or influencer commission
rows.text: The default rate.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Sales agent or B2B broker commission
rows.text: The default rate.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Startup Contingency Fund
rows.text: A share of the Total Pre-operational Budget, 10 to 15%. It is held when operations start.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Operational Contingency Fund
rows.text: A share of a month's OpEx, 3 to 5%, set aside each month after the launch until the target is reached. A cash set-aside, held as savings.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Target operating reserve
rows.text: Months of OpEx the Operational Contingency Fund builds up to. 3 by default; an investor may ask for 6.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Channel Fee Table
rows.text: What each channel takes of its sales: revenue x (commission + chargeback allowance) + the fixed fee x orders. The rates are examples; edit them once here.
scenes: Global Settings

rows.label: Early Positioning
rows.text:
Who is your target audience: who pays, and who uses it?
Why do they buy it: what purpose does it serve?
How you stand apart is asked on your Segments, under their Competitors.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Early Positioning

rows.label: Seller & Buyer Relationship
rows.text:
Who pays: the buyer who approves the budget; the person who uses it can be someone else.
The positioning statement is written for the buyers; each distinct group of them may need its own.
B2C (Business-to-Consumer): individuals or consumers who pay for personal or family use.
B2B (Business-to-Business): businesses, companies, freelancers or public bodies.
At this stage (Planning): choose one. When the stage changes (the Opening Date), an answer over the limit goes back to empty.
Based on: Stayman, D. (2015) ‘How to Write Market Positioning Statements’, eCornell #IMPACT, Cornell University, 20 March. Available at: https://ecornell-impact.cornell.edu/how-to-write-market-positioning-statements/ (Accessed: 25 October 2026).
Also: Loy, T. (2007) E145 Technology Entrepreneurship, Session 6: Entrepreneurial Marketing. Stanford, CA: Stanford University. Available at: https://web.stanford.edu/class/e145/2007_fall/startup_mktg_details.shtml (Accessed: 25 October 2026).
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Early Positioning

rows.label: Audience Specialisation & Scale
rows.text:
How big the businesses you sell to are. Your Segment's size question offers the sizes that go with it.
Solopreneurs & Freelancers: individual professionals (immediate decision, need for low cost or self-service).
Startups & SMBs: small and medium-sized or rapidly growing companies (need for speed, flexibility and an immediate solution).
Mid-Market: medium-sized businesses with structured departments (need for workflows, roles and scale).
Enterprise or Public Sector: multinationals or public bodies (multi-month sales or tender cycle, need for maximum security).
At this stage (Planning): choose one. When the stage changes (the Opening Date), an answer over the limit goes back to empty.
Based on: U.S. Small Business Administration (n.d.) Market research and competitive analysis. Available at: https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/plan-your-business/market-research-competitive-analysis (Accessed: 25 October 2026).
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Early Positioning

rows.label: Buyer's category
rows.text:
What the buyer buys for. It tells the buyer who pays from the person who uses it, whatever the buyer's life stage or scale.
Direct Buyers: purchasing exclusively for their own personal use.
Proxy Buyers: purchasing exclusively on behalf of someone else (a gift, a parent buying for a child, an employer buying for its staff).
Dual-Intent Buyers: purchasing a single offering to be used by themselves and their dependents (a family plan, a shared tier).
For Proxy and Dual-Intent Buyers the questions about the end user follow.
At this stage (Planning): choose one. When the stage changes (the Opening Date), an answer over the limit goes back to empty.
Based on: The Open University (n.d.) ‘3.4 Business decision makers’, in Understanding your customers. Milton Keynes: The Open University (OpenLearn). Available at: https://www.open.edu/openlearn/money-business/understanding-your-customers/content-section-3.4 (Accessed: 26 October 2026).
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Early Positioning

rows.label: Purpose
rows.text:
Why the offering is bought: the purpose it serves for the person who gets it.
Only the purposes that fit your answers above are offered: the primary ones first, then the possible ones.
At this stage (Planning): choose one. When the stage changes (the Opening Date), an answer over the limit goes back to empty.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Early Positioning

rows.label: Founders & Ownership
rows.text: Who the founders are, how much of the organisation each owns, and what each brings to it.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Founders & Ownership

rows.label: Roles
rows.text:
What does this founder do in the organisation?
One role a line: a founder is often several things at once.
Lenders and investors look for every key job to have someone who owns it.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Founders & Ownership

rows.label: Relevant Industry Experience
rows.text:
Which relevant companies, sectors, positions, projects or markets have they worked in?
Say how long, where it helps.
Lenders and investors look for a team that already knows the market it is entering.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Founders & Ownership

rows.label: Management Experience
rows.text:
Say how big it was: how many people, how much money and for how long.
It shows they can run the organisation as it grows.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Founders & Ownership

rows.label: Key Achievements
rows.text:
One achievement a line, with a figure where there is one: sales, customers, savings.
Any business they started before, and how it turned out.
Results are what make a track record believable.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Founders & Ownership

rows.label: Skills, Expertise & Qualifications
rows.text:
Add one entry for each, and choose its type.
Name what the plan relies on them for: sales, finance, operations, technical.
Lenders and investors check that every capability the plan needs is covered by someone.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Founders & Ownership

rows.label: Mission
rows.text:
Who do you serve? What do you do for them? Why does it matter to them?
Say what you do today; the future you aim for belongs in the Vision.
Make it specific enough to describe your business alone.
Example: "We weave personalised throws that let people give a gift that lasts."
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Mission &Vision

rows.label: Vision
rows.text:
What will be different for your customers when you succeed, and what will the business be by then?
Think five to ten years ahead. Describe the result; the steps belong in the Strategy.
Example: "Every home in the UK and Ireland has one throw it keeps for life."
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Mission &Vision

rows.label: Organisation
rows.text: Choose the country first: the legal forms, the registry and the activity codes follow it.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Organisation

rows.label: Legal Form
rows.text:
Decides who is liable for the organisation's debts: the organisation, or you personally.
Decides how it is taxed, and whether it must hold share capital.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Organisation

rows.label: Opening Date
rows.text:
The day the business opens and issues its first receipt. It sets the stage: planning before it, launching from it.
The stage also sets Positioning's name and how many choices its questions allow; a change of stage empties an answer over the new limit.
Costs dated before it make the pre-operational budget, on the Financial Foundation.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Organisation

rows.label: Activities
rows.text: The first is the primary activity; add others, up to four in all. Each one ends in one official code of your country (the NAICS code).
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Organisation

rows.label: Notes
rows.text:
Who are you, and what do you do? What do you create or provide?
Write it as a registry or a bank would expect to read it.
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Organisation

rows.label: Philosophy
rows.text:
What do you believe about your trade that sets you apart? Why do you work this way?
Explain the belief; the rules it leads to go in Principles.
Example: "We believe a thing made slowly is used for longer, so we make fewer and better."
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Philosophy &Manifesto

rows.label: Manifesto
rows.text:
What do you stand for, and what do you stand against?
Write it for your customers, in your own voice. Draw on your Values and say them in fresh words.
Example: "We are for things that last. We are against the throwaway gift."
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Philosophy &Manifesto

rows.label: Values
rows.text:
What matters most in how you work? What would you hold to, even at the cost of a sale?
List three to five, one a line, each with what it means here.
Example: "Craft: every piece is finished by hand and checked before it leaves."
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Values &Principles

rows.label: Principles
rows.text:
For each value, what do you always do, and what do you always avoid?
One rule a line, beginning "We …".
Example: "We remake any piece with a fault, at no cost, within a year."
scenes: Identity System / 1. Definition / tile Values &Principles

rows.label: Gaps
rows.text: The capabilities the plan needs that the team lacks today.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Capability

rows.label: Cover
rows.text:
For each gap, say who covers it and from when.
A gap that is named and covered reads as a strength; one left unnamed reads as a risk.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Capability

rows.label: Expenses
rows.text:
What it costs to register and keep registered: filing, renewal and agent fees. Each is linked to one registration or requirement.
Licences, insurance and certificates for an offering are recorded in Documents & Rights, on 3. Infrastructure & Capability.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Expenses
Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Expenses / card 1

rows.label: Expenses
rows.text:
What it costs to register and keep registered: filing, renewal and agent fees. Each is linked to one registration or requirement.
Licences, insurance and certificates for an offering are recorded in Documents & Rights, on 3. Infrastructure & Capability.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Expenses / card 1

rows.label: Linked registration
rows.text:
Says which registration or requirement this expense pays for.
It lists the registration numbers and the requirements recorded under Registrations.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Expenses / card 1

rows.label: Authority / Name
rows.text:
The body that keeps the public register your organisation is on; on a further row, the name of that registration.
Filled in from the country you chose; for another country, write it.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Registrations / card 1

rows.label: Tax Identification Number (EIN)
rows.text:
The number the tax office knows the organisation by.
In some countries it is the registration number; in others it is issued separately when you register for tax.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Registrations / card 1

rows.label: Sales Tax
rows.text:
Sales Tax is a tax on sales: you add it to your prices, pay it to the tax authority and reclaim what you paid on your purchases.
Registration is required once your sales pass the threshold your country sets, and some businesses can register by choice. Check with your tax authority.
Ticked, it asks for your number, and the Financial Foundation reads your amounts as excluding Sales Tax unless you choose otherwise.
scenes: Identity System / 2. Legal Entity / tile Registrations / card 1

rows.label: Current Situation
rows.text:
What do you sell, and who uses it? (3. Business System → 1. Foundation: Offerings and Customer Segments)
How do people discover and reach you? (3. Business System → 2. Customer Engagement: Customer Channels)
How are you supported financially today? (3. Business System → 4. Financial Foundation: Costs and funding; 5. Sustainability: Revenue and break even)
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Current Situation

rows.label: Refresh
rows.text: Filled in from the Business System. Edit it freely.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Current Situation

rows.label: Strategic Compass
rows.text:
Where do you want your organisation to be heading, and what do you want it to build, become, or achieve over the long term?
Choose a time horizon far enough ahead to give your strategy direction, yet close enough for your organisation to make meaningful decisions about.
The Vision is the goal; the Compass is the route.: A future in which every small professional firm can use automation and AI as safely and confidently as a large one. Ten years from now, Quillfield is a trusted name for practical automation among small firms across the north-east United States: a small team of automation specialists, a library of proven and well-documented workflows, and hundreds of client firms whose staff spend their days on skilled work. Success means clients who stay for years, recommend us to their peers and never feel locked in.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Compass

rows.label: Strategic Period
rows.text:
Choose a start and an end: three to five years.
Name 3 to 5 Strategic Themes: broad areas the organisation intends to develop during the strategic period.
Say briefly why each Theme matters.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period
Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 1
Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 2

rows.label: Adding Themes
rows.text:
Growth & Market: Focus on expanding the organisation's customer base, market presence, reach, or overall scale.
Customers & Experience: Focus on acquiring, retaining, understanding, and creating greater value for customers, including improving their overall experience.
Products & Innovation: Focus on developing, improving, expanding, or innovating the organisation's products, services, offerings, or intellectual property.
Revenue & Financial Sustainability: Focus on building sustainable revenue, improving profitability, managing costs, strengthening cash flow, and achieving financial stability.
Brand & Positioning: Focus on strengthening brand recognition, differentiation, reputation, market positioning, and the organisation's relationship with its audience.
Operations & Capability: Focus on improving operational efficiency and developing the people, systems, technology, resources, and capabilities required to execute the strategy.
Partnerships & Expansion: Focus on developing strategic partnerships, entering new markets or locations, and creating new opportunities through external relationships.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period
Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 1
Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 2

rows.label: Theme
rows.text: A broad area the organisation intends to develop during the Strategic Period (for example Financial Stability, or a Recurring Client Base). A Theme holds Goals; a Goal holds Objectives, and an Objective its Initiatives and Metrics.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 2

rows.label: Goal
rows.text: What do you want to accomplish within each Strategic Theme, and why does it matter?
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 2

rows.label: Objective
rows.text: Specific, measurable, and time-bound milestones that support a Goal.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 2

rows.label: Initiatives
rows.text: Actions focused on major areas of work to achieve the Objectives.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 2

rows.label: Metric
rows.text: Measures that provide evidence of progress toward the Objective.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile Strategic Period / card 2

rows.label: SWOT Analysis
rows.text:
Strengths and Weaknesses: inside your organisation.
Opportunities and Threats: outside, in your market.
Think of resources, skills, customers, competition and technology.
scenes: Strategy System / main / tile SWOT Analysis
